title: Sentence Improvement
summary: One highlighted segment per sentence must be corrected — or left alone ('No substitution required'). The same fault families recur as error-spotting (agreement, tense, comparison, prepositions, inversion), so the elimination ladder — verb form, agreement, structure, word choice, economy — resolves most items in under thirty seconds.

subtopics.title: The elimination ladder: how to choose in 20 seconds
subtopics.concept:
Sentence improvement gives you a sentence with one highlighted segment and four substitutes (often including 'No substitution required'). You are not hunting for the *best-sounding* English — you are hunting for the option that survives every grammatical test the original failed.

**Work the ladder top to bottom; eliminate as you descend:**

| Rung | Question | What it kills |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Verb form & tense | is the highlighted verb the right form for its anchor and helper? | tense clashes (with 'yesterday'), wrong form after did/have, non-finite where finite is needed |
| 2. Agreement | does the verb match the TRUE subject? | plural verbs after 'each', 'one of', 'the list of', 'as well as' |
| 3. Structure | is word order and pairing standard (inversion, that of, correlative pairs)? | broken inversions, mixed pairs, compared-with-itself errors |
| 4. Word choice & idiom | is the preposition/word the fixed partner? | insisted for, angry on, return back |
| 5. Economy | does any option say the same thing in fewer, cleaner words? | redundant add-ons — but beware over-pruning |

**The three-option rule:** in most items, two options die instantly on rung 1 (wrong verb form) or rung 2 (agreement). That leaves a pair; rung 3 or 4 separates them. Practise announcing WHY an option dies — 'fails agreement', 'breaks the pair', 'wrong preposition partner' — and the ladder becomes automatic.

**'No substitution required' discipline:** before accepting it, run rungs 1–3 once. It is correct in roughly a quarter of such items — a real option, not a decoy. But never choose it because the sentence merely sounds acceptable; if the highlighted verb disagrees with its subject, 'sounds fine' is irrelevant.

**When two options both seem right:** prefer the one that is *closer to the original in meaning*. The exam improves grammar, not the writer's ideas. An option that subtly changes who did what, or adds information, is wrong even if its grammar is clean.

**Timing:** 20–30 seconds. Read the full sentence first — the part BEFORE the highlight usually carries the anchor (yesterday, did, each, no sooner) that decides everything.

tricks.title: Anchor before options
tricks.body: Find the time word or helper verb near the highlight ('yesterday', 'did', 'each of the'), decide what the verb must look like, then pick the option matching YOUR form.

example.q: She **has met** him yesterday evening. Options: met / has meet / was met / No substitution required.
example.solution: Anchor 'yesterday' = finished past → simple past 'met'. Option 1; the other two fail rung 1 outright.

tricks.title: Death-note elimination
tricks.body: In your head, tag every option with its fatal flaw before choosing: 'plural verb', 'breaks inversion', 'wrong partner'. If no option has a flaw, the answer is 'No substitution required'.

tricks.title: Meaning guard
tricks.body: Between two grammatical survivors, choose the one that preserves the original meaning word for word — the exam rewards accuracy, not elegance.

mistakes: Choosing a grammatical option that changes the meaning (active↔passive swap, added agents).
Picking 'No substitution required' because the sentence sounds natural at speed.
Improving a part that was never highlighted — only the bold segment may change.
Overlooking the anchor in the unhighlighted part of the sentence.
subtopics.notes:
### What sentence improvement asks
One segment of the sentence is printed in bold. Four substitutes are offered, usually including **No substitution required**. Your job: decide whether the bold part is faulty, and if it is, pick the substitute that repairs it — and only it.

### The elimination ladder (four rungs)
1. **Name the highlighted part's job.** Is it a verb, a tense, an article + noun, a preposition, a connector, a comparison phrase? The job tells you which rulebook page to open.
2. **Run the matching rule.** Verb → agreement and tense anchors; article → sound rule; connector → fixed pairs. If the bold part survives its own rule, check whether any other rule touches it.
3. **Kill the repeat-fault options.** Many options repeat the very fault you are fixing (*more better → more good*). Kill them at once; they are not competitors.
4. **Kill the new-fault options.** Some options repair fault A but plant fault B (*Hardly…than* instead of *Hardly…when*). A substitute must be cleaner than the original, not differently wrong.
5. If the bold part is standard English, choose **No substitution required** without hesitation.

### The two-fault trap
Examiners build one option that fixes the visible fault and breaks a hidden rule:
- *My friend has gone to Delhi yesterday.* → the fault is *has gone* with *yesterday*; the fix is **went**. *Had gone* also removes the perfect, but it creates a wrong sequence (nothing earlier exists to outrank). One fix, two faults removed — that is the answer's test.

### Decoy families
Options usually come in families around the bold word:
- **Sound-alike / look-alike**: *effect / affect, loose / lose, advice / advise.*
- **Form-shifts**: adjective ↔ adverb (*brave / bravely*), noun forms (*braveness*).
- **Marker-doubles**: *more better, most shortest, more preferable.*
- **Helper-swaps**: *has / had / was / did* in every combination.
Learn to name the family; the correct option is the family member that matches the rule.

### Smallest-change principle
When two options both fix the fault, prefer the one that changes less. Exams reward the repair, not a rewrite. If an option replaces the whole structure while another fixes one word, test the one-word fix first.

### Timing
Improvement items are fast: 30 to 40 seconds. Read the sentence once fully, name the job, run the rule, walk the ladder.

### Quick revision
- Name the job of the bold part → open the matching rulebook page.
- Kill options that repeat the fault; kill options that plant a new fault.
- *No substitution required* is a full citizen — choose it when the original is standard.
- Watch decoy families: effect/affect, brave/bravely, more better, helper swaps.
- Two options both fix the fault? The smaller, cleaner change wins.

patterns.name: Single-fault fix with repeat-fault decoys
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part has one clear fault; two or three options repeat the same fault in a new dress (more good for more better, was being for were).
patterns.logic:
1. Name the fault and its rule.
2. Strike out every option that still breaks that same rule.
3. Compare the survivors — pick the clean, smallest repair.

*Why it works:* repeat-fault decoys punish candidates who fix the fault only in their head and stop reading the options.

example.q: "The quality of the mangoes (were) not satisfactory this season." was / have been / No substitution required / are being
example.solution: True subject = quality (singular) → **was**. 'Have been' and 'are being' repeat the plural fault; strike them out, then compare *was* with the original.

patterns.name: No-substitution discipline
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part is already standard English; the other options are 'repairs' that break it.
patterns.logic:
1. Run the full rule check on the bold part itself.
2. If it passes every rule (tense anchor, agreement, pair, comparison), do not invent work.
3. Choose **No substitution required** and move on.

*Why it works:* papers include 2-3 correct originals per set; changing a correct sentence is the most common self-inflicted error.

example.q: "She (has been teaching) in this school since 2015." teaches / is teaching / No substitution required / has taught
example.solution: Perfect continuous + *since 2015* + still continuing → **has been teaching** is exactly right. Every offered change breaks the frame → No substitution required.

patterns.name: Decoy families around the bold word
patterns.howToSpot: The options are near-twins of the bold word: adjective/adverb pairs, noun forms, effect/affect-type twins.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the job of the slot: describing a noun or an action?
2. Cut the family members that do the wrong job (adverb where an adjective sits).
3. Of the survivors, keep the one whose meaning fits the sentence.

*Why it works:* option families are built from one word's relatives; sorting them by job (not by sound) clears the set.

example.q: "The soldier was praised for his (brave) act during the rescue." bravely / No substitution required / braveness / bravest
example.solution: The slot describes the noun *act* → adjective: **brave** is correct. *Bravely* (adverb), *braveness* (noun) and *bravest* (wrong count) are the family decoys → No substitution required.

patterns.name: Two-fault trap options
patterns.howToSpot: One tempting option fixes the visible fault but plants a second one (a wrong sequence, a broken pair, a wrong part of speech).
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the visible fault in your head first.
2. Test every option that seems to fix it against the OTHER rules in the sentence (time words, pairs, count).
3. Reject any option that needs a second repair; keep the option that leaves the sentence fully standard.

*Why it works:* 'has gone yesterday → had gone yesterday' *feels* fixed; only the second pass exposes the new sequence fault.

example.q: "My friend (has gone) to Delhi yesterday to attend an interview." went / had gone / No substitution required / has went
example.solution: The anchor *yesterday* demands simple past → **went**. 'Had gone' removes the perfect but creates a sequence with no earlier event; 'has went' keeps the fault and adds another.

subtopics.title: Tense and sequence fixes
subtopics.concept:
A large share of improvement items highlight a verb whose tense contradicts a visible anchor.

**Anchor → required form:**
- *yesterday, last week, in 2010, ago* → simple past; any perfect form is wrong.
- *since/for + still true* → perfect or perfect continuous: *has been living since 2015* (not *is living* / *lived*).
- *already/just* with an earlier past event → past perfect: *had left*.
- *when/if/until* with future meaning → simple present in the clause, *will* in the main clause only.
- reported speech after a past reporting verb → backshift AND statement word order: *asked why I **had left*** (not *why did I leave*).

**Test the pair, not the word:** tense errors are relative. The highlighted verb must agree in time with its neighbour. Read the whole sentence across the highlight, never the highlight alone.

**Continuous vs simple:** continuous forms need an ongoing frame. *She **was cooking** when the guests arrived* is right; *She **cooked** when the guests arrived* changes the meaning (two sequential events). Improvement questions exploit exactly this contrast — pick the form that preserves the original meaning.

tricks.title: Yesterday test
tricks.body: See a finished-time anchor? Kill every perfect and continuous option instantly — one survivor usually remains.

example.q: The train **has left** before we reached the station.
example.solution: Both events are past; the earlier needs past perfect → *had left*. 'Has left' is present perfect — dead on rung 1.

tricks.title: Backshift + straight order
tricks.body: In reported questions after *asked/told*, two things must change: tense backshifts and the question flips to statement order ('why he had left'). Each option usually breaks exactly one of the two — check both.

tricks.title: Since/for health check
tricks.body: 'Since 2015 / for ten years' demands a perfect form with *been* if the action continues. Options without *have/has been* die at once.

mistakes: Choosing present perfect with 'yesterday/last year' because it 'sounds formal'.
Backshifting tense but keeping question order (or vice versa) in reported speech.
Replacing a correct perfect with simple past when 'since/for' is present.
Changing continuous to simple (or back) and silently altering the meaning.
subtopics.notes:
### The anchor decides, again
In improvement items the bold part is often a verb whose tense fights a visible anchor. Circle the anchor before touching the options.

| Anchor in the sentence | Required form |
|---|---|
| yesterday, last week, ago, in 2019 | simple past |
| since + point, for + length, so far, already, yet | perfect (or perfect continuous) |
| every day, at nine (habit) | simple present |
| when / if / until + future meaning | simple present inside the clause |
| by the time + past, earlier of two past events | past perfect |
| said / asked / told (past reporting) | backshifted past forms |

### Reported speech: two rules, not one
1. **Backshift**: after a past reporting verb, move the tense one step back — *has locked → had locked*, *will → would*, *is → was*.
2. **Statement order**: an indirect question loses question order — *asked why **he was** late* (never *why was he late*), and takes one connective only — *asked **whether*** (never *that whether*), *asked **why*** (never *that why*).

### Conditional frames travel in pairs
- Real future: **if + present, will + verb** → *If he apologises, I will withdraw the case.*
- Unreal present: **if + past (were for all persons), would + verb** → *If I were the collector, I would act.*
- Unreal past: **if + had + participle, would have + participle** → *If he had studied, he would have cleared.*
The bold verb may sit in either half; check that the pair matches one row of the table.

### Since / for with continuing action
*Since 2015, for twenty years, since childhood* + an action still true → **has/have been + -ing**: *He has been working in the same mill for twenty-two years* (not *is working*). The anchor *for + length* cannot live with the plain present continuous.

### Watch the second verb too
Some sentences carry two verbs and the anchor governs both. *He **has left** for Delhi and **will return** next month* — the anchor *next month* is future, so *will return* is right, and nothing else in the sentence pulls *has left* into the past. But *He **has left** for Delhi and **will return** next week* with *when he **will reach***… breaks: the when-clause must read *when he reaches*. After substituting the bold verb, glance at the unbolded verbs once — a fix that clashes with them is not a fix.

### How improvement differs from error-spotting
Here the wrong form is already underlined — your task is to produce the right form, not to find it. So after every fix, re-read the WHOLE sentence once: a substitute that fixes the verb but clashes with a word outside the bold part is a trap.

### Quick revision
- Circle the anchor first; the verb obeys it.
- ago / yesterday → simple past; since + point → perfect; for + length + continuing → has been -ing.
- Reported questions: backshift + statement order + one connective (why / whether).
- Conditionals come in three fixed pairs; match the pair, don't mix halves.
- Re-read the whole sentence after substituting — the trap may sit outside the bold part.

patterns.name: Anchor-based tense fix
patterns.howToSpot: The bold verb's tense contradicts a time word sitting in plain sight (already, yesterday, by the time, every morning).
patterns.logic:
1. Circle the anchor.
2. Read the anchor's required form off the table.
3. Pick the option that matches; reject options that shift tense again (has → had) without a second event.

*Why it works:* tense questions are anchor questions; with the anchor circled, the options sort themselves.

example.q: "When I reached the station, the train (already left)." had already left / has already left / No substitution required / already leaves
example.solution: The train left BEFORE I reached → earlier past event → **had already left**. *Has already left* reaches into the present and breaks the past story.

patterns.name: Reported-speech backshift and order fix
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence reports what someone asked or said (asked, told, enquired) and the bold part keeps question order, misses the backshift, or glues 'that' to a wh-word.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the past reporting verb.
2. Backshift the tense one step; restore statement order (subject before helper).
3. Keep exactly one connective: why / whether / if.

*Why it works:* indirect speech is direct speech pushed through two fixed machines — backshift and order — and options break one machine each.

example.q: "The teacher asked the boy (why was he) late again." why he was / No substitution required / why is he / that why he was
example.solution: Indirect question → statement order + backshift: asked **why he was** late again. 'Why was he' keeps question order; 'that why' glues two connectives.

patterns.name: Conditional half repair
patterns.howToSpot: An if-sentence has mismatched halves: will inside the if-clause, or a real-future frame where an unreal one is meant (If I was → were).
patterns.logic:
1. Read both halves of the conditional.
2. Match them to one of the three fixed pairs.
3. Real future takes if + present; unreal present takes were; unreal past takes had + participle.

*Why it works:* the if-clause never hosts will (real future) or would have (unreal past); the options exploit exactly these two guests.

example.q: "If he (will apologise) sincerely, I will withdraw the complaint." apologises / No substitution required / would apologise / apologised
example.solution: Real future condition → if + **apologises**; the main clause keeps *will withdraw*. 'Would apologise' is the unreal-present form and breaks the pair.

patterns.name: Since / for with a continuing action
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence names a starting point or a length of time (since 1998, for twenty years) while the bold verb is in a plain present or present continuous.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: does the action still continue? (since + a past point usually says yes.)
2. Continuing action → has/have been + -ing (or has/have + participle for states).
3. Reject the plain present and the continuous that ignores the length.

*Why it works:* the perfect exists to tie a past starting point to now; the plain present cuts the tie.

example.q: "My father (is working) in the same mill for twenty-two years." has been working / No substitution required / works / had been working
example.solution: *For twenty-two years* + still employed → **has been working**. The plain continuous drops the 'still going' meaning that the length demands.

subtopics.title: Agreement and verb-form fixes
subtopics.concept:
When the highlighted segment is (or contains) a verb, run the agreement audit: find the TRUE subject.

**Interrupters that never change number:** *of the..., as well as, along with, together with, in addition to, accompanied by, and not, besides*. The verb follows the first, real subject:
- *The list of candidates **was** displayed* (list).
- *One of the students **has** won* (one).
- *The captain, as well as the players, **was** fined* (captain).

**Always-singular subjects:** *each, every, everyone, everybody, either, neither, nobody, one*. Always-plural in effect: *cattle, police, people*.

**Verb form after helpers:** after *did/does/do* → base form; after *have/has/had* → past participle; after *be* → *-ing* (continuous) or participle (passive). Improvement items highlight the wrong slot of this chain: *did he **arrived*** → *did he arrive*.

**There is/there are:** the verb agrees with the noun AFTER it — *There **is** a temple and two shops* is acceptable SSC usage when the first noun governs; but standard items usually keep simple agreement with the real subject, so audit that noun first.

tricks.title: Cover the phrase, read the skeleton
tricks.body: Physically cover 'of the candidates'-type phrases with a finger and read what remains: 'The list ___ displayed'. The agreeing verb is now obvious.

example.q: One of the students **have** won the quiz. Options: has / were / are / No substitution required.
example.solution: Skeleton: 'One ___ won' → has. Plural options die on rung 2.

tricks.title: Helper-chain audit
tricks.body: did → base, have → participle, be → -ing/participle. When the highlight contains a helper, check the partner form first — that is where the planted error lives.

tricks.title: Two-subject sentence check
tricks.body: If two subjects are joined by *and*, the verb is plural — unless the pair names one thing ('bread and butter **is**'). SSC plants singular verbs before such pairs.

mistakes: Agreeing with the nearest noun instead of the head subject.
Writing a participle where the base form belongs after *did*.
Choosing a passive-looking option that adds or deletes an agent and changes meaning.
Marking plural verbs correct after 'each of the + plural noun' because the plural noun is nearer.
subtopics.notes:
### The audit: find the true subject
When the bold part contains (or ends in) a verb with a helper — *was/were, has/have, is/are, does/do* — run the agreement audit:
1. **Find the true subject**: the noun the sentence is about.
2. **Cross out the interrupters**: phrases that begin with *of, with, along with, as well as, together with, besides, including* never contain the subject.
3. **Match the helper** to the subject's number.

### Interrupters that hide the subject
- *The bundle of old files **was** sent*… (bundle, not files)
- *The captain, as well as the openers, **was** blamed*… (as-well-as adds; it does not make a plural)
- *The quality of the mangoes **was** poor.*
- *The list of holidays **has been** announced.*

### One-of / each-of / neither-of — singular, always
- *One of my cousins **has settled** in Wellington.*
- *Each of the candidates **is** to report at nine.*
- *Neither of the two answers **was** acceptable.*

### Nearness rule for paired subjects
With *either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject:
- *Either the secretary or the joint secretaries **are** responsible.*
- *Not only the students but also the wardens **were** honoured.*

### Quantity and collective phrases
- **A number of** + plural noun → plural verb: *A number of films **have been** censored this month.*
- **The number of** → singular: *The number of films **has** fallen.*
- **Many a** + singular noun → singular: *Many a farmer **has** shifted to drip irrigation.*
- Amounts as one unit → singular: *Ten thousand rupees **is** a big amount.*
- Collective nouns (jury, committee) → usually singular with *its*.

### Compound subjects and the passive
Two nouns joined by plain *and* take a plural helper: *The principal and the secretary **were** present* (two people). But one person with one article is singular: *The principal and secretary **was** present* (one person holding both posts). In the passive, the same audit runs on the *be* helper: *The bridge **was** built* (singular subject) but *The bridges **were** built*. The helper is always the first place to look, because it moves with the subject while the participle never changes.

### In improvement format
The bold part usually holds only the helper (*was / were / has / have*) or helper + participle. Fix the helper to the true subject and keep the rest of the bold part untouched — the smallest change wins. If the original already agrees, **No substitution required** is the answer.

### Quick revision
- of / with / along with / as well as → never the subject; the noun BEFORE the phrase is.
- one of, each of, neither of, many a → singular helper.
- either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also → nearer subject.
- a number of → plural; the number of → singular; amounts as units → singular.
- Fix only the helper; leave the participle alone unless it too is faulty.

patterns.name: Interrupter-phrase agreement fix
patterns.howToSpot: The bold helper (was/were, has/have) sits after 'X of Y' or 'X, as well as Y,' and was matched to the wrong noun.
patterns.logic:
1. Cross out the of/with/as-well-as phrase.
2. Read the sentence with only the true subject and the helper.
3. Pick the helper that matches the subject's number, leaving the participle untouched.

*Why it works:* the interrupter is designed to be heard as the subject; crossing it out removes the illusion.

example.q: "The captain, as well as the openers, (were) blamed for the collapse." was / No substitution required / have been / are
example.solution: The subject is **the captain**; 'as well as the openers' only adds information → the captain **was** blamed. The plural helpers repeat the illusion.

patterns.name: One-of / each-of / neither-of fix
patterns.howToSpot: The subject phrase begins with one of, each of, or neither of, and the bold helper is plural.
patterns.logic:
1. Remember the head word: one, each, neither — all singular.
2. The plural noun after 'of' is a decoy.
3. Choose the singular helper (has, is, was).

*Why it works:* these three openers are unconditionally singular, so the fix is mechanical once you see the opener.

example.q: "Each of the shortlisted candidates (are) to report by nine tomorrow." is / No substitution required / were / have been
example.solution: **Each** → singular → each **is** to report. 'Were' and 'have been' follow the plural noun, not the opener.

patterns.name: Nearness-rule fix (or / nor / not only…but also)
patterns.howToSpot: Two subjects are joined by either…or, neither…nor, or not only…but also, and the bold helper agrees with the FIRST subject instead of the nearer one.
patterns.logic:
1. Ignore the first subject.
2. Look at the subject just before the bold helper.
3. Match the helper to that nearer subject.

*Why it works:* the nearness rule outranks every other consideration in paired subjects, and the setter always makes the two subjects differ in number.

example.q: "Either the secretary or the joint secretaries (is) responsible for the circular." are / No substitution required / was / has been
example.solution: Nearer subject = joint secretaries (plural) → **are** responsible. 'Is' and 'was' follow the distant 'secretary'.

patterns.name: Quantity-phrase agreement fix (a number of / many a)
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is a quantity phrase — a number of, the number of, many a — and the helper's number contradicts the phrase's rule.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the phrase slowly: a number of (plural) or the number of (singular)?
2. many a + singular noun → singular, despite the plural meaning.
3. Match the helper, keep the rest of the bold part as it is.

*Why it works:* the article before 'number' is one letter of print with full control of the verb; 'many a' hides a singular under a plural meaning.

example.q: "A number of films (has been) censored this month." have been / No substitution required / are been / was
example.solution: **A number of** = many → plural: a number of films **have been** censored. ('The number of films has…' would be the singular frame.)

subtopics.title: Comparison and structural fixes
subtopics.concept:
**Comparison fixes.** Two recurring shapes:
1. Double marker: *more better, most fastest* → drop the extra word (*better, fastest*).
2. Unlike things compared: *The climate of Shimla is cooler than **Delhi*** → compare climate with climate: ***that of* Delhi**. Singular possession → *that of*; plural → *those of*. This tiny pronoun is one of SSC's favourite right answers.

**Structural fixes** are about standard shapes:
- Inversion after negative openers: *Hardly **had I reached**... when...*, *No sooner **did he arrive** than...*, *Not only **did she sing**, but she also danced*. The highlighted segment is usually the un-inverted half.
- Correlative pairs kept parallel: *not only + verb ↔ but also + verb*; *both... and*; *either... or*.
- Dangling modifiers: an *-ing* opener must describe the subject that follows. *Walking through the park, the flowers attracted the child* → the child must become the subject: *Walking through the park, **the child was attracted by the flowers***.
- Word order in embedded questions: *He asked **why I had left*** (statement order).

**The repair must be minimal.** Among options that fix the fault, SSC's key is the smallest correct change. An option that rewrites half the sentence is usually there to distract.

tricks.title: that-of insertion
tricks.body: When two possessive phrases are compared and only the second is highlighted, 'that of / those of' is almost always the answer. Check number: singular → that of, plural → those of.

example.q: The roads of Bhopal are wider than **Indore**. Options: those of Indore / that of Indore / Indore's roads are / No substitution required.
example.solution: Roads (plural) vs roads → *those of Indore*.

tricks.title: Negative-opener flip
tricks.body: See *Hardly/No sooner/Not only/Little* at sentence start? Expect auxiliary-before-subject order in the highlighted part: 'had I reached', 'did he arrive'. Un-inverted options die on rung 3.

tricks.title: -ing opener ownership
tricks.body: Ask WHO is doing the -ing action. The sentence's main subject must be that doer; if not, pick the option that makes the doer the subject.

mistakes: Choosing 'than that of' when the comparison is not possessive at all.
Inverting a clause that has no negative opener.
Fixing a dangling modifier by moving the modifier instead of changing the subject.
Treating 'No substitution required' as wrong whenever the sentence looks plain — plain and correct are different things.
subtopics.notes:
### The four comparison repairs
1. **Double marker**: *more better, most shortest, more preferable* → drop the extra word (*better, shortest, preferable*). A comparative or superlative is already marked; never mark it twice.
2. **Like with like (that of / those of)**: compare the same kind of thing. *The climate of Shimla is cooler than **that of** Delhi* (climate with climate); *The roads of Bhopal are wider than **those of** Indore* (roads with roads). *That* for a singular noun, *those* for a plural.
3. **Latin comparatives take to**: *senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to, prior to, preferable to, prefer X to Y* — never *than*.
4. **Count the items**: exactly two → comparative (*the larger of the two*); three or more → superlative (*the largest of the five*). *Of all…* → superlative.

### How the options are built
- One option repeats the fault with new paint: *more better → more good*; *senior than → more senior than*.
- One option fixes the marker but breaks the count: *the most effective* kept where only two items exist.
- One option replaces *than Delhi* with a full clause (*Delhi's streets are*) — this produces a doubled sentence and is never the cleanest repair.
- The clean repair changes only what the fault requires.

### Words that are already marked
Some words carry their degree inside them and refuse extra markers: *better, worse, elder, former, latter, major, minor, superior, inferior, prior, senior, junior, preferable, perfect, unique, ideal, complete.* Say *better*, never *more better*; say *unique*, never *most unique* — a unique thing has no scale to climb. When such a word sits in the bold part, the correct option is almost always the plain form, and the decoys add *more/most* to it.

### Counting traps
The count is often announced inside the sentence: *of the two routes*, *of all the models*, *one of the finest*. Read that phrase before judging the form. *Of all* demands -est/most; *of the two* demands -er/more.

### Whole-sentence check
After substituting, re-read: the fix must not create a second fault. *Those of* with a singular noun, *prefer to* with *than* still trailing, or a superlative left without *the* — each is a new fault wearing the old fix's clothes.

### Quick revision
- more better / most shortest → cut the doubled marker.
- climate vs city → that of (singular) / those of (plural).
- senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable → TO; prefer → TO.
- of the two → comparative; of all → superlative (with the).
- Reject options that fix the marker but break the count, or turn the sentence into a doubled clause.

patterns.name: Double-marker fix
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part contains more + -er or most + -est (more better, far more better, most shortest).
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the marked form (better, shortest).
2. Delete the doubled marker — the fix is a subtraction, not a substitution.
3. Reject options that swap one doubling for another (more good) or destroy the comparison (good).

*Why it works:* the double marker is pure redundancy; the correct option is the one that simply stops marking twice.

example.q: "The second model is (far more better) than the first." far better / No substitution required / more good / best
example.solution: **Far better** keeps the intensifier and drops the doubled marker. 'More good' re-doubles; 'best' breaks the two-item frame with *than*.

patterns.name: That-of / those-of repair
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence compares 'the X of A' with a bare place or person ('than Delhi', 'than most cereals'), so unlike things are being compared.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the two things being compared.
2. They must be the same kind: X with X.
3. Insert that of (singular X) or those of (plural X) before the second item.

*Why it works:* 'the roads of Bhopal vs Indore' compares roads with a city; *those of* quietly rebuilds the missing 'the roads of'.

example.q: "The streets of Mysuru are cleaner than (Bangalore)." those of Bangalore / that of Bangalore / No substitution required / Bangalore's streets
example.solution: Streets (plural) vs streets → **those of Bangalore**. *That of* is singular; 'Bangalore's streets are' doubles the clause.

patterns.name: Latin comparative / prefer repair
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part pairs senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable (or prefer) with than (or another wrong partner).
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the Latin comparative or *prefer*.
2. Its partner is **to**, always.
3. Reject options that keep *than* in any dress (more senior than) or switch the meaning (prefer to → liking).

*Why it works:* these words came into English with their own preposition attached; *than* belongs only to -er/more comparatives.

example.q: "My sister (prefers coffee than) tea in winter." prefers coffee to / No substitution required / prefer coffee to / is preferring coffee than
example.solution: **Prefer X to Y**: prefers coffee **to** tea. 'Prefer coffee than' keeps the fault; the bare 'prefer' loses the -s agreement.

patterns.name: Count-of-items repair (two vs three-plus)
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence announces the count (of the two, of all, of the five) and the bold form has the wrong degree.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the count phrase (of the two / of all).
2. Two → comparative with the; three or more → superlative with the.
3. Pick the option with the right degree and keep *the* in place.

*Why it works:* the degree is not a style choice — the announced count fixes it, and the options include the neighbouring degree as the decoy.

example.q: "Iron is (the most useful) of the two metals for construction." the more useful / No substitution required / more useful / useful most
example.solution: **Of the two** metals → comparative: **the more useful**. 'The most useful' would need three or more metals; 'more useful' drops the required *the*.

subtopics.title: Precision fixes: articles, prepositions, pronouns, word choice
subtopics.concept:
Some highlights contain no verb at all — the fault is a wrong *small word* or a wrong *word pair*.

**Articles:** sound decides *a/an* (*an hour, a university, an MLA*); specificity decides *the* (*the same, the most intelligent, the Ganga*). Improvement items usually highlight the article-plus-noun together: *She is **a honest** woman* → *an honest woman*.

**Prepositions:** recall the governor's fixed partner — *insist on, apologize to... for, angry with (person), good at, married to, prefer to, depend on, consist of*. The wrong partner is planted; the right partner is the answer.

**Pronoun case:** after prepositions → object form (*between you and **me***); as reflexive only when the subject and object are the same person (*She cooked herself lunch*) — *myself* cannot replace *me/I* in ordinary sentences, a favourite decoy.

**Word choice and redundancy:**
- redundant pairs die: *return back → return*, *repeat again → repeat*, *revert back → revert*.
- confusables flip meaning: *few/a few, little/a little, much/many, fewer/less* — the improvement item asks which one the sentence's logic needs ('There is **a little** water left' = some, positive).
- *elder* (family, no *than*) vs *older than*; *farther* (distance) vs *further* (additional).

**One-word economy:** between two correct options, the standard written form wins — *because* over *due to the fact that*, *although* over *despite of the fact that* ('despite of' is itself wrong: *despite* or *in spite of*).

tricks.title: Small-word sweep
tricks.body: Read ONLY the small words in the highlight (a/an/the, in/on/at, I/me/myself). A wrong one usually stands alone in its wrongness — fix it and finish.

example.q: She is **a honest** woman. Options: an honest / the honest / honest / No substitution required.
example.solution: Vowel sound 'o' in *honest* → *an honest woman*. 'Honest' alone would leave 'She is honest woman' — ungrammatical.

tricks.title: myself firewall
tricks.body: Reflexives never replace plain object pronouns. Any option offering *myself* where *me* belongs is a decoy — kill it on sight.

tricks.title: Redundancy flinch
tricks.body: Train on the fatal pairs: return back, repeat again, revert back, final conclusion. When one appears highlighted, the shorter option is the key.

mistakes: Choosing 'the' before a superlative-less unique noun or dropping it where it belongs.
Picking 'myself' as a polite-sounding substitute for 'me'.
Correcting *few* to *a few* (or back) without reading whether the sentence means 'some' or 'hardly any'.
Writing 'despite of' — the standard forms are *despite* and *in spite of*.
subtopics.notes:
### Small words, big marks
Many bold parts contain no verb at all — the fault is an article, a preposition, a doubled word, or a swapped twin. The options then differ by one or two small words, and speed comes from knowing the fixed pairs cold.

### Article: sound rule
- Vowel SOUND → an: *an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an X-ray.*
- Consonant sound → a: *a university, a European, a one-day match.*
- *A ancient route → **an** ancient route* (the a/an swap is the entire question).

### Preposition partners (frozen pairs)
- approve **of**, insist **on**, fond **of**, afraid **of**, capable **of**
- agree **with** (person) / **to** (proposal), angry **with** (person) / **at** (thing)
- apply **to** (office) / **for** (post), abide **by**, comply **with**
When the bold part is only the preposition, recall the partner and choose it — meaning will tempt you toward the wrong one.

### Redundancy: cut the echo
*revert back → revert; return back → return; repeat again → repeat; wrote back a reply → wrote a reply; final conclusion → conclusion.* One idea, one word. In improvement items the fix is a subtraction — the correct option is simply shorter.

### Swapped twins
| Wrong twin | Right twin | Why |
|---|---|---|
| advise (noun slot) | advice | advice = noun, advise = verb |
| effect (verb slot) | affect | affect = verb, effect = noun |
| loose (misplace) | lose | loose = not tight |
| principal (rule of conduct) | principle | principle = a rule |

### More pairs to keep ready
- **win / beat**: India *beat* Australia (beat takes the opponent); India *won* the match (win takes the prize).
- **say / tell**: she *said* that…; she *told me* that… (tell needs a person).
- **hear / listen**: *hear* is accidental; *listen to* is deliberate — *listen to the news*.
- **die of / die from**: *die of* a disease, *die from* an injury.
- **comprise**: the team *comprises* eleven players (no *of*); *is comprised of* in formal prose.
- **cope with**, deal with, but **cope up with is wrong** — a favourite Indian-English decoy.

### Pronoun case after prepositions
*Between you and **me*** (not I); *for **him** and **me***. The reflexive (*myself*) cannot replace the object pronoun — it is the standard decoy.

### Method
1. Name the small word's job (article? preposition? adverb of the pair?).
2. Recall the rule or pair.
3. Prefer the option that changes only the faulty word. If the bold part is already standard, choose **No substitution required**.

### Quick revision
- an hour, an MLA — a university, a European: sound, not spelling.
- approve of, insist on, fond of, agree with a person / to a plan.
- revert back, return back, repeat again → cut the echo.
- advice (n) / advise (v); affect (v) / effect (n); lose / loose.
- between you and me; myself never replaces me.

patterns.name: Preposition-partner repair
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part is (or contains) the preposition after a verb or adjective, and the options are preposition swaps.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the verb/adjective the preposition hangs on (approve, insist, fond).
2. Recall its fixed partner: approve OF, insist ON, fond OF.
3. Ignore options that change the rest of the phrase — only the partner needs repair.

*Why it works:* preposition questions are memory questions; the partner is not chosen by logic but by usage.

example.q: "The committee does not approve (for) the proposal." of / No substitution required / with / to
example.solution: The fixed pair is approve **of** → 'does not approve of the proposal'. The other prepositions belong to different verbs.

patterns.name: Article sound repair
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part is an article + word where the article contradicts the word's first sound (a honest, an useful, a MLA).
patterns.logic:
1. Say the word after the article aloud.
2. Vowel sound → an; consonant sound → a.
3. Ignore the spelling — *hour* and *university* are the classic traps.

*Why it works:* the rule follows speech, and exam words are picked so the letter and the sound disagree.

example.q: "The temple was built near (a ancient) trading route." an ancient / No substitution required / a ancients / the ancients
example.solution: **Ancient** begins with a vowel sound → **an ancient** trading route. Only the article needs repair — the smallest change wins.

patterns.name: Redundancy cut
patterns.howToSpot: The bold part carries an echo — return back, revert back, repeat again, wrote back a reply — and the correct option is simply shorter.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: does one word already contain the other's meaning?
2. The repair is a subtraction: keep the single strong word.
3. Reject options that keep the echo or alter the tense while 'fixing' it.

*Why it works:* the echo feels natural in speech, so the eye skips it; the shorter option only looks too plain.

example.q: "Please (revert back) to my mail by Friday." revert to / No substitution required / revert back to / reversing to
example.solution: **Revert** already means 'come back' (in exam usage, reply) → *revert to my mail*. 'Back' is the echo; cut it and keep *to*.

patterns.name: Swapped-twin repair
patterns.howToSpot: The bold word is the wrong member of a twin pair: advice/advise, effect/affect, lose/loose, principal/principle.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the slot's job: noun or verb?
2. Map the job to the twin: advice (n) / advise (v); affect (v) / effect (n).
3. Reject options that change the form further (advising, effecting) — the twin alone repairs the sentence.

*Why it works:* both twins are real words, so nothing looks misspelt; only the part-of-speech test convicts the wrong one.

example.q: "The doctor's (advise) was to rest for a week." advice / No substitution required / advises / advising
example.solution: The slot is a noun (the subject of 'was') → the doctor's **advice**. *Advise* is the verb; *advising* changes the structure.

subtopics.title: Structural fixes: inversion, dangling modifiers, parallelism
subtopics.concept:
Some highlights fail not in tense or agreement but in *sentence architecture*. Three shapes cover the exam.

**Inversion after negative openers.** When *Hardly, Scarcely, No sooner, Not only, Little, Never, Rarely* opens the sentence, the auxiliary jumps before the subject:
- *Hardly **had I reached** the office when...* (past perfect pairs with *when*);
- *No sooner **did he arrive** than...* (base form after *did*, partner *than*);
- *Not only **did she sing**, but she also danced* (parallel verbs on both halves).
The un-inverted order ('I had reached', 'he arrived') is the planted fault.

**Dangling modifiers.** An *-ing* or participle opener must describe the sentence's main subject. *Walking through the garden, **the flowers** fascinated the boy* — flowers cannot walk. The repair makes the true doer the subject: *Walking through the garden, the boy was fascinated by the flowers*. Reject fixes that merely move the opener around; the subject must change.

**Parallelism under pairs and lists.** *Not only X but also Y* needs X and Y in the same grammatical shape (verb with verb, noun with noun, clause with clause). The same holds for *either... or*, *neither... nor*, *both... and*, and for item lists (*reading, writing, and to speak* → *speaking*).

**Embedded-question order.** Inside a reported question the statement order returns: *He asked **why I had left***, never 'why did I leave'. Improvement items highlight exactly this stretch.

Each of these fixes is a *shape*, not a judgement call — memorise the four shapes and the correct option announces itself.

tricks.title: Opener triggers flip
tricks.body: Negative word first? Then expect 'auxiliary + subject': had I reached, did he arrive, did she sing. Choose the option in flipped order with the right partner (when/than).

example.q: No sooner he **arrived** than the power failed. → did he arrive
example.solution: *No sooner* + inversion + base form after *did* + *than*: the full shape must be present, not part of it.

tricks.title: Who is doing the -ing?
tricks.body: Name the doer of the opening action; if the main subject is not that doer, pick the option that promotes the doer to subject.

tricks.title: Shape-match across pairs
tricks.body: Cover the pair words and compare the shapes on both sides: 'not only [verbed] ... but also [verb]' — any mismatch in form is the fault being tested.

mistakes: Inverting a clause with no negative opener, or forgetting to invert when there is one.
Pairing 'Hardly... than' or 'No sooner... when' — the partners are fixed.
Fixing a dangling modifier by rewording the opener instead of changing the subject.
Ignoring parallelism: 'not only cheap but also it lasts long' mixes adjective with clause.
subtopics.notes:
### Inversion: when the helper jumps first
Certain opening words force the helper BEFORE the subject:
- **No sooner … than**: *No sooner **had the train left** than the TTE began checking.*
- **Hardly / Scarcely … when**: *Hardly **had the results been announced** when the servers crashed.*
- **Negative adverbs** (never, seldom, rarely, little, nowhere): *Never **have I witnessed** such a peaceful poll.*
The frame is fixed: opener + helper + subject + main verb + partner word (than for no sooner, when for hardly/scarcely). Options break one part at a time — statement order, wrong partner, wrong helper — so test the three parts separately.
Both *no sooner* frames are legal: *No sooner **did he arrive** than…* and *No sooner **had he arrived** than…* — but each half must match its own frame.

### Dangling modifiers: the opener must describe the subject
An -ing or being opener borrows the main clause's subject:
- Wrong: ***Being a rainy day**, the mela was cancelled.* (The mela was not a rainy day.)
- Right: ***It being a rainy day**, the mela was cancelled.* (Or: *Because it was a rainy day…*)
- Wrong: *Having eaten our lunch, **the train** departed.* (The train ate nothing.)
- Right: *Having eaten our lunch, **we boarded** the train.*
Test: who performs the opener's action? That doer must be the subject.

### Parallelism: one shape down the list
Items joined by and/or/but keep one form: *typing, filing papers, and drafting mails* — not *typing, to file papers, and how to draft mails*. Correlatives too: *not only intelligent but also hardworking* — the words after *not only* and *but also* must be the same kind.

### Word order after reporting verbs
*Asked why **he was** late* — statement order, no *that*, backshifted tense. The improvement options usually offer the question order as a decoy.

### Two more structure repairs
- **Misplaced *only***: *only* sits before the word it limits. *Only he accompanied me* (nobody else came) vs *He accompanied only me* (nobody else was accompanied). Improvement options move *only* around; pick the spot that matches the intended sense.
- **Split infinitives and heavy splits**: keep the marker with its verb when the exam offers it — *to examine carefully* is safe; the exam rarely wants a rewrite here, so prefer **No substitution required** unless the order is truly wrong.

### Method for structure items
1. Find the opener or the connector that controls the architecture.
2. Recall its fixed frame (inversion order, doer of the -ing, list shape).
3. Pick the option that satisfies the frame — usually the one that reorders, not the one that rewords.

### Quick revision
- No sooner…THAN; hardly/scarcely…WHEN; opener forces helper-first order.
- Never/seldom/rarely at the front → inversion (Never have I seen).
- An -ing/being opener describes the main subject; if it cannot, rewrite with It being… or name the doer.
- Lists and correlatives stay parallel — same shape for every item.
- Reported questions: statement order + backshift, no 'that'.

patterns.name: No-sooner / hardly frame repair
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with No sooner or Hardly/Scarcely and the bold part (or its neighbourhood) shows statement order, a wrong partner (than vs when), or a mismatched helper.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the frame: no sooner…THAN; hardly/scarcely…WHEN.
2. Check the order: opener + helper + subject + verb.
3. Check the helper-verb match (had + participle, did + base).
4. Both 'no sooner' shapes are legal (had left / did leave) but each must stay inside its own frame.

*Why it works:* the frame has three parts, and each wrong option breaks exactly one.

example.q: "No sooner (the train had left) the platform than the TTE began checking tickets." had the train left / No substitution required / the train had left / the train had leave
example.solution: **No sooner** demands inversion: no sooner **had the train left** than… 'The train had left' keeps statement order; 'had leave' breaks the participle.

patterns.name: Negative-adverb inversion repair
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with never, seldom, rarely or little and the bold part keeps normal statement order (I have, we see).
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the negative adverb at the front.
2. Invert: helper + subject + main verb (Never **have I** witnessed).
3. Keep the tense; only the order changes.

*Why it works:* fronted negatives pull the helper forward in standard English; the decoys reorder nothing and merely change tense.

example.q: "Never (I have) witnessed such a peaceful poll in this constituency." have I witnessed / I had witnessed / No substitution required / I have witness
example.solution: Fronted **Never** → inversion: never **have I witnessed**. Only the order changes; the tense stays present perfect.

patterns.name: Dangling-modifier repair
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence begins with an -ing or being phrase, and the main-clause subject cannot be the doer of that phrase (Being a rainy day, the mela…).
patterns.logic:
1. Ask who performs the opener's action or state.
2. If the main subject cannot be the doer, the sentence dangles.
3. Pick the option that names the doer as subject, or converts the opener to 'It being…' / a full clause.

*Why it works:* English attaches the opener to the nearest noun; the repair either changes the subject or gives the opener a subject of its own.

example.q: "(Being a rainy day), the mela was cancelled by the committee." It being a rainy day / No substitution required / Being rainy day / Been a rainy day
example.solution: The mela cannot *be* a rainy day → **It being a rainy day**, the mela was cancelled. The absolute construction gives the opener its own subject.

patterns.name: Parallelism repair in lists and correlatives
patterns.howToSpot: A list joined by and/or, or a not only…but also pair, mixes shapes: two -ing items and one to-item, or an adjective on one side and a clause on the other.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the items in a column.
2. Match each item's shape to the first.
3. Pick the option that makes every item copy the same form — usually the uniform -ing list or the paired adjectives.

*Why it works:* readers parse a list as one unit; the correct option restores one shape so the unit parses cleanly.

example.q: "The training module covers (typing, to file papers, and how to draft mails)." typing, filing papers, and drafting mails / No substitution required / typing, filing papers, and to draft mails / typing, to file papers and draft mails
example.solution: Every item must be an -ing form: **typing, filing papers, and drafting mails**. The mixed shapes break the parallel line.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part is a verb and the sentence carries a visible time anchor — already, yesterday, by the time, every morning, since 2015.
pyqPatterns.approach: Circle the anchor and read off the required form: ago and yesterday demand simple past; the earlier of two past events takes had + participle; habits take the simple present; a since/for phrase with a continuing action takes has been -ing. Then reject options that shift tense again without a second event.

example.q: When I reached the station, the train (already left). Options: had already left / has already left / No substitution required / already leaves.
example.solution: The leaving happened before the reaching, so the earlier event takes the past perfect: had already left.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part holds a helper verb (was/were, has/have) sitting after an 'of…' phrase, an as-well-as phrase, or a one-of / each-of / neither-of opener.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cross out the interrupting phrase and find the true subject; match the helper to it and leave the participle untouched. For either…or and not only…but also, agree with the nearer subject; a number of takes a plural verb, the number of a singular one.

example.q: The captain, as well as the openers, (were) blamed for the collapse. Options: was / No substitution required / have been / are.
example.solution: 'As well as' only adds information — the subject stays the captain: was blamed.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A past reporting verb (asked, told, enquired, wanted to know) is followed by a bold part in question order, an unshifted tense, or 'that why / that whether'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Push the direct sentence through two machines: backshift the tense one step, and restore statement order (subject before helper). Keep exactly one connective — asked why, asked whether; 'that' never joins a wh-word.

example.q: The teacher asked the boy (why was he) late again. Options: why he was / No substitution required / why is he / that why he was.
example.solution: Indirect questions take statement order plus backshift: why he was late again.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part shows a doubled marker (more better), a bare place after 'than' (than Delhi), a Latin comparative with than (senior than), or the wrong degree for the announced count (the most useful of the two).
pyqPatterns.approach: Cut the doubled marker; compare like with like using that of / those of; give Latin comparatives and prefer their partner to; count the items — of the two takes the comparative, of all takes the superlative.

example.q: The streets of Mysuru are cleaner than (Bangalore). Options: those of Bangalore / that of Bangalore / No substitution required / Bangalore's streets.
example.solution: Streets must be compared with streets, plural: those of Bangalore.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part is a small word after a verb or adjective (approve for, insisted for) and the options swap prepositions, or the sentence contains an echo like revert back / repeat again.
pyqPatterns.approach: Treat verb + preposition as one memorised chunk — approve of, insist on, fond of, comply with — and pick the partner. For echoes, the repair is a subtraction: return, repeat and revert already contain the idea of back or again, so the correct option is the shorter one.

example.q: Please (revert back) to my mail by Friday. Options: revert to / No substitution required / revert back to / reversing to.
example.solution: Revert already means come back — cut the echo: revert to my mail.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part is an article + noun (a honest, an useful) or a single twin word in the wrong job (advise for advice, effect for affect).
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the next word aloud: vowel sound → an (an hour, an MLA), consonant sound → a (a university). For twins, decide the slot's part of speech: advice is the noun and advise the verb, affect the verb and effect the noun — then keep the change to one word.

example.q: The temple was built near (a ancient) trading route. Options: No substitution required / an ancient / a ancients / the ancients.
example.solution: Ancient begins with a vowel sound: an ancient trading route.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Inversion repair (no sooner / hardly / negative adverbs)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with No sooner, Hardly/Scarcely, Never or Seldom, and the bold part keeps statement order, uses the wrong partner (than vs when), or mismatches helper and verb.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the fixed frames: no sooner…THAN and hardly/scarcely…WHEN both force helper-first order (no sooner had he left / no sooner did he leave); fronted never and seldom invert with the helper or do-support (never have I seen, seldom do we see). Test order, partner word and helper-verb match as three separate checks.

example.q: No sooner (the train had left) the platform than the TTE began checking tickets. Options: had the train left / No substitution required / the train left / the train had leave.
example.solution: No sooner demands inversion: no sooner had the train left than…

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The sentence begins with an -ing or being phrase whose doer is missing or impossible (Being a rainy day, the mela…; Having eaten our lunch, the train…), or a list and a not only…but also pair mix shapes.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ask who performs the opener's action; that doer must be the main subject, or the opener needs its own subject (It being a rainy day). For lists, make every item copy the first item's shape — uniform -ing items or paired adjectives.

example.q: (Being a rainy day), the mela was cancelled by the committee. Options: It being a rainy day / No substitution required / Being rainy day / Been a rainy day.
example.solution: The mela cannot be a rainy day: give the opener its own subject — It being a rainy day.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The bold part already passes every rule — a correct tense, a correct pair, a correct article — while every option quietly breaks one.
pyqPatterns.approach: Run the full check on the bold part before touching the options; if it survives its own rules, choose No substitution required without inventing work. Papers plant two or three correct originals per set to punish both the over-fixers and the blind pickers.

example.q: She (has been teaching) in this school since 2015. Options: teaches / is teaching / No substitution required / has taught.
example.solution: Perfect continuous with since 2015 and still continuing is exactly right: No substitution required.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

She **has met** him yesterday evening.
solvedExamples.solution: The anchor *yesterday evening* fixes finished past time, so the simple past **met** is required; present perfect (*has met*) cannot sit beside a finished-time adverbial. *Has meet* is doubly wrong (no third form), and *was met* turns the meaning into a passive. Ladder: rung 1 kills three options in one stroke.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Finished-time anchor (yesterday) → simple past. One check, three options dead.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The climate of Shimla is cooler than **Delhi**.
solvedExamples.solution: A comparison must compare like with like: climate with climate. *That of Delhi* = 'the climate of Delhi' — singular *that* matches singular *climate*. *Those of* is plural and cannot replace a singular noun's possession, and 'Delhi's climate is' produces a doubled clause ('the climate ... is cooler than Delhi's climate is') that changes the structure. Ladder: rung 3 (standard structural shape).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Two possessive phrases compared + only the second highlighted → 'that of' (singular) / 'those of' (plural).

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

He has been working in this office **since** 2015 without a single complaint.
solvedExamples.solution: *Since* + a point of time (*2015*) with a continuing perfect continuous is exactly standard: rungs 1–4 find no fault. *For* takes durations (*for eight years*), *from* needs a endpoint framing and no perfect, *by* marks deadlines. When the original is standard, **No substitution required** is the answer — and it must be chosen with the same confidence as any other option.
solvedExamples.shortcut: If every rung finds no flaw, mark 'No substitution required' and move on — do not second-guess.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The list of selected candidates **were** displayed on the notice board.
practice.solution: The true subject is *list* (singular); 'of selected candidates' is an interrupter. → *was displayed*. Plural options fail agreement; the original fails too.
practice.shortcut: Cover 'of the candidates': 'the list ___' → was.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

One of the students **have** won the inter-college quiz.
practice.solution: *One* is the subject: 'One of the students **has** won'. The plural noun *students* sits inside the interrupting phrase.
practice.shortcut: Skeleton 'one ___' → has.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

This new road is **more better** than the old one.
practice.solution: *Better* is already comparative; *more* doubles the marker. → *better than the old one*. 'More good' repeats the fault, and 'good' destroys the comparison entirely.
practice.shortcut: Double comparative: delete the extra marker, keep the comparative.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The roads of Bhopal are wider than **Indore**.
practice.solution: Compare roads with roads: plural noun → **those of Indore**. *That of* is singular and wrong here; 'Indore's roads are' creates a doubled clause; 'No substitution required' leaves an unlike comparison.
practice.shortcut: Plural possession compared → those of; singular → that of.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

She insisted **for** paying the full fare before boarding.
practice.solution: *Insist* takes **on**: 'insisted on paying'. The gerund after the preposition is correct, so only the partner is at fault.
practice.shortcut: Governor chant: insist—on.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

After serving abroad for a decade, he **returned back** to his hometown.
practice.solution: *Return* already means 'come back'; *back* is redundant → **returned**. 'Was returned' changes the meaning to a passive (someone sent him).
practice.shortcut: Redundant pair: return + back → keep the simple verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Between you and **I**, this welfare scheme has several loopholes.
practice.solution: A preposition takes object forms: *between you and **me***. *Myself* is a reflexive and cannot replace *me* — a favourite decoy.
practice.shortcut: Preposition + I → flip to me; never accept 'myself' as a fix.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

My grandmother is **a honest** and hardworking woman.
practice.solution: *Honest* begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent): **an honest**. 'The honest' over-specifics the generic sentence; 'a honestly' is wrong twice (article and part of speech).
practice.shortcut: Silent-h words take 'an'.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

No sooner he **arrived** than the power supply failed.
practice.solution: *No sooner* at the start demands inversion + *than*: **did he arrive** (base form after *did*). 'Had he arrive' mixes the *had* inversion with a base form, and 'he did arrive' is not inverted.
practice.shortcut: No sooner → did + subject + base verb + than.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Hardly **I had reached** the office when the fire alarm went off.
practice.solution: *Hardly* opening the sentence forces auxiliary-first order: **had I reached** (past perfect pairs with *when*). 'Did I reached' pairs *did* with a past form; 'I had reach' keeps statement order and breaks the participle.
practice.shortcut: Hardly/Scarcely at sentence start → had + subject + participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Walking through the garden, **the flowers** fascinated the little boy.
options: the little boy fascinated the flowers
the little boy was fascinated by the flowers
practice.solution: The *-ing* opener (*walking*) must describe the main subject. Flowers cannot walk, so the boy must become the subject: *Walking through the garden, **the little boy was fascinated by the flowers***. 'The little boy fascinated the flowers' reverses who fascinated whom; 'the flowers were fascinating' keeps the dangling structure; 'No substitution required' leaves it unfixed.
practice.shortcut: -ing opener: ask WHO walks — make that doer the subject.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The manager asked me **why did I** leave my previous job without notice.
practice.solution: After the past reporting verb *asked*, an indirect question needs statement order + backshift: **why I had** left. 'Why had I' backshifts nothing and keeps question order; 'that why I' wrongly glues *that* to *why*; the original commits both faults.
practice.shortcut: Reported question: tense backshifts AND word order straightens.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

He has been living in Chennai **since** 2015 and has no plans to move.
practice.solution: *Since* + point of time with a continuing perfect is standard: rungs 1–4 find no fault. *For* needs a duration (*for nine years*), *from* and *by* do not pair with this perfect. → **No substitution required**.
practice.shortcut: Since = point, for = span. The original is standard; trust it.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Neither of the two answers **were** acceptable to the examiner.
practice.solution: *Neither* is singular → **was** acceptable. 'Have been' and 'are' repeat the plural fault; the original fails agreement.
practice.shortcut: Neither/either/each → singular verb, always.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

My elder brother is **two years senior** than me in service.
practice.solution: Latin comparatives (*senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior*) take **to**, never *than*: *two years senior to me*. 'More senior than' doubles the comparison; 'senior of' is not a form.
practice.shortcut: senior/junior/superior/inferior/prefer + to. Memorise the family of five.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Neither of the two ministers **were present** at the cabinet meeting.
practice.solution: **Neither** is singular; *ministers* sits inside the 'of' phrase → neither **was present**. 'Were being' repeats the plural fault, and 'has been present' breaks the simple-past narration.
practice.shortcut: neither of → singular.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The quality of the mangoes **were** not satisfactory this season.
practice.solution: The subject is **quality**; 'of the mangoes' is an interrupter → quality **was** not satisfactory. 'Have been' and 'are being' repeat the plural fault.
practice.shortcut: cover the 'of' phrase; quality is singular.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The chairman, along with the directors, **were** inspecting the plant when the auditors arrived.
practice.solution: 'Along with' only adds information; the subject stays **the chairman** → **was inspecting**. The narration is past, so the present helpers in options 3 and 4 are out at once.
practice.shortcut: along with → first subject decides.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

She **has been teaching** in this school since 2015.
practice.solution: Perfect continuous + *since 2015* + still continuing is exactly standard → **No substitution required**. Every offered change breaks the frame: *teaches* drops the duration, *is teaching* drops the start point, *has taught* weakens the continuing sense.
practice.shortcut: since + continuing action → has been -ing; do not repair a correct sentence.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The court **annulled** the election of two sitting legislators last week.
practice.solution: The anchor *last week* demands the simple past — **annulled** is correct → No substitution required. 'Has annulled' clashes with the finished time, 'was annulled' reverses the meaning, 'annuls' breaks the time frame.
practice.shortcut: last week → simple past; rung discipline: check before repairing.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

**Having finished** the audit, the chartered accountant left for Madurai.
practice.solution: The perfect participle **having finished** correctly marks the earlier action, and the doer (the accountant) is the main subject → No substitution required. The other options break the participle structure entirely.
practice.shortcut: having + participle is standard for the earlier of two actions.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The manager gave us **an useful** tip about saving fuel.
practice.solution: **Useful** begins with a consonant sound (yoo-) → **a useful** tip. The decoy family tests the same slot three ways: 'an usefully' is wrong twice (article + part of speech), 'the useful' over-specifies a general tip.
practice.shortcut: u with a y-sound → a.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The cyclone **effected** the coast badly last November.
practice.solution: The slot needs the verb 'to influence' → **affected**. 'Has effected' keeps the wrong twin AND clashes with *last November*; 'was affected' reverses who did what.
practice.shortcut: affect = verb, effect = noun; keep the anchor in view.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The soldier was praised for his **brave** act during the rescue.
practice.solution: The slot describes the noun *act* → the adjective **brave** is correct → No substitution required. The decoy family offers the adverb (*bravely*), the noun (*braveness*) and an impossible superlative.
practice.shortcut: adjective before a noun; resist form-shift decoys.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

My friend **has gone** to Delhi yesterday to attend an interview.
practice.solution: The anchor *yesterday* demands the simple past → **went**. 'Had gone' removes the perfect but creates a sequence fault (no earlier event exists); 'has went' keeps the fault and adds a wrong form — both are two-fault traps.
practice.shortcut: fix the fault AND leave no new one behind.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Scarcely had the minister **sat down than** the journalists stood up.
practice.solution: The pair is **scarcely…when** → 'scarcely had the minister **sat down when**…'. Option 1 fixes the partner but breaks the tense (after *had*, the participle *sat* is required); option 4 keeps the wrong partner — both are two-fault traps.
practice.shortcut: scarcely…WHEN; a fix must not plant a second fault.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The number of complaints **have risen** since the new fare came into force.
practice.solution: **The number of** → singular → the number **has risen**. 'Has raised' fixes the number but breaks transitivity (*raise* needs an object); 'have raised' fixes nothing — two-fault traps on both sides.
practice.shortcut: the number of → singular; rise (no object) vs raise (object).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

When I reached the station, the train **already left**.
practice.solution: The train left BEFORE I reached — the earlier of two past events takes the past perfect → **had already left**. 'Has already left' pulls the story into the present; the original loses the sequence.
practice.shortcut: earlier past event → had + participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The shop **will open** at nine every morning.
practice.solution: *Every morning* marks a habit → the simple present: the shop **opens** at nine. *Will open* treats a routine as a one-off future decision.
practice.shortcut: habitual anchor → simple present.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

By the time the doctor arrived, the patient **died**.
practice.solution: 'By the time + past' points to an action completed before the later past event → the patient **had died**. 'Was dying' changes the meaning (he was in the process, not dead); the original erases the sequence.
practice.shortcut: by the time + past → past perfect for the earlier event.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Ravi told the inspector that he **has locked** the godown the previous night.
practice.solution: Past reporting verb (*told*) + a past reference point (*the previous night*) → backshift to the past perfect: he **had locked**. Plain 'locked' ignores the earlier-of-two structure; 'was locking' changes the meaning.
practice.shortcut: told that + earlier past action → had + participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The teacher asked the boy **why was he** late again.
practice.solution: An indirect question needs statement order + backshift: asked **why he was** late again. 'Why is he' keeps both faults; 'that why' glues two connectives.
practice.shortcut: asked + wh-word + subject + verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

She enquired **that whether** the parcel had reached the branch office.
practice.solution: A reported yes/no question takes ONE connective: **whether** (or if). 'That whether' and 'that if' stack two; 'if whether' does the same in reverse.
practice.shortcut: one connective only: whether / if.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

If he **will apologise** sincerely, I will withdraw the complaint.
